turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You know as well as I do, Mr. Darcy, that your interference in Mr. Wickham's affairs was unwarranted and unjust. Your actions have caused nothing but harm and suffering to those around you, and I will not be swayed by empty declarations of love when you have shown such a blatant disregard for the well-being of others.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, I find it quite astonishing that you would presume to lecture me on the subject of justice and morality, considering the numerous instances in which you have displayed a blatant disregard for propriety and the well-being of those around you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How dare you imply that I have disregarded propriety? I have acted with integrity and principle, whereas you have consistently demonstrated a lack of both.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must say, Miss Elizabeth, that your indignation at my supposed lack of principle is quite laughable, considering the numerous instances in which you have compromised yourself in the eyes of society.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You have the audacity to suggest that I have compromised myself? How can you possibly know what I have done, when you are so clearly blinded by your own prejudices and misconceptions?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, I find your manner of expression to be quite distressing, Miss Elizabeth. Your tone and language are those of a person deeply offended, but I fail to see the justification for such emotion.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You are so accustomed to having your own way and imposing your will on others that you have lost all sense of what is truly just and decent. I will not be lectured by someone who has consistently demonstrated such a lack of understanding and compassion.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Miss Elizabeth, that you refrain from making such scathing accusations against me, as they are entirely unfounded and unjust. My actions, though perhaps not always agreeable to you, have been guided by a sense of duty and responsibility to those under my care. I will not be maligned by your baseless invective.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You may have convinced yourself that your actions have been guided by duty and responsibility, but I see only a desire to control and manipulate those around you, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, your obstinacy is quite astonishing, Miss Elizabeth. It is most unbecoming in a young woman of your station and breeding.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am astonished that you can continue to protest your innocence with such conviction, Mr. Darcy, when the evidence of your actions is so clear.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Miss Elizabeth, that you are not in a position to judge my character or motivations, when your own behavior has been so rash and impulsive, often to the detriment of those around you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not surprised that you would try to shift the blame onto me, Mr. Darcy. You have a history of attempting to justify your own behavior, no matter how egregious.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am at a loss to understand why you continue to harbor such unfounded resentments towards me, Miss Elizabeth.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not harbouring unfounded resentments, Mr. Darcy. You have consistently demonstrated a lack of regard for the well-being of those around you, and I will not be swayed by empty professions of love or affection.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I daresay, Miss Elizabeth, your own feelings towards me are a subject of great interest, and I must confess that I find it quite incomprehensible that you do not see the sincerity of my affections.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not interested in your declarations of affection, Mr. Darcy, nor do I believe them. Your actions have consistently demonstrated a lack of principle and a disregard for those around you, and I will not be swayed by empty words.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: You mistake the nature of my feelings, Miss Elizabeth, and I must confess that I find it quite distressing to be rejected in such a manner, after having made such a frank and sincere declaration of my affection.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not surprised that you find my rejection distressing, Mr. Darcy, for I daresay it is a rare experience for you to be met with a lack of enthusiasm for your own interests and opinions.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I find your continued obstinacy and refusal to consider my affections to be quite perturbing.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
